segments: Tarrow Marsh is a mile of mudflat, creek and cordgrass on a quiet coast, and it is the only known home of the banded marsh crab, an animal no wider than a thumbnail.

Each summer the flats swarm with the crabs. Each October they disappear, and for more than a century nobody could say where they went.

The storm of 1953 is remembered at Tarrow for one lasting change:
During the long search for the crabs, researchers worked from the marsh's field station, a small hut at the landward edge.

The search began in earnest in 2016, when the ecologist Peter Halloran and his team glued tiny numbered tags to two hundred crabs each September. For three winters the tagged animals simply vanished. In the fourth,

After more than a century, the crabs' winter hiding place was finally known.

Much of the fieldwork in those winters fell to Mara Sollis, who had joined the project as an unpaid volunteer when she retired at sixty.

Halloran still calls her the best recruit the project ever had.

Halloran's team is now planning a fifth winter on the flats.
